summary: Argentina classifies the roof rat (Rattus rattus) as a Category 1 Invasive Exotic Species (EEI-1, 'especie restringida y de control obligatorio') under Resolución 109/2021. Article 5 of that resolution imposes a blanket federal ban on the breeding (cría), purchase/sale, donation, release, importation, and inter-jurisdictional movement of EEI-1 species — so breeding, selling/giving, and transport of a roof rat are prohibited, with no lawful permit pathway (the Art. 5 ban preempts the otherwise-available fauna-operator registry of Res. 170/2021). Private possession ('tenencia') of a pre-existing captive-bred specimen sits in a deliberate gap: Art. 5 enumerates banned actions but omits passive possession, and the constitutional legality principle (Const. Nacional Art. 19) means no one can be deprived of what the law does not forbid — so keeping is best read as unregulated/unclear rather than expressly legal, and a province or municipality could still add a local ban. The brown/fancy rat (R. norvegicus) is taxonomically EEI-1 too, yet is sold and kept openly thanks to a de-facto domestication exemption — an exemption R. rattus, lacking any recognized domestic lineage, does not enjoy.

kit.problem: In Argentina the roof rat (Rattus rattus) is listed as a Category 1 Invasive Exotic Species (EEI-1) under Resolución 109/2021. Article 5 of that resolution bans the breeding, sale, donation, release, import, and inter-jurisdictional movement of EEI-1 species, and because the species is EEI-1 the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad has no authority to issue a breeder/operator license for it — so the otherwise-available fauna-operator registry (Res. 170/2021) is foreclosed. The striking part is that the common fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) carries the IDENTICAL EEI-1 listing, yet it is bred, transported, and sold openly nationwide because authorities treat its century-old laboratory/fancy strains as domestic animals (animales domésticos) outside the wildlife regime. R. rattus simply never received that institutional recognition, so a tame, captive-bred roof rat is hit with the full force of the invasive-wildlife prohibitions purely on the basis of its species name. Separately, private possession ('tenencia') is conspicuously absent from the Art. 5 ban list, leaving a captive owner in a gray zone — not prosecuted for merely keeping the animal, but unable to lawfully breed, give, sell, or move it.
kit.ask: Ask the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad to confirm in writing (a) that passive private possession of a pre-existing captive-bred Rattus rattus, kept indoors and never released, is not among the activities banned by Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021; and (b) whether a formal regulatory exception exists or can be granted — via Art. 6 of Res. 109/2021, an internal dictamen, or administrative jurisprudence — that extends to captive-bred, closed-colony R. rattus the same de-facto 'domestic animal' treatment already afforded to R. norvegicus, so that documented captive-bred specimens fall outside the EEI-1 commercialization/transport prohibitions. For anyone importing, ask SENASA whether an EEI-1-classified companion rodent is automatically rejected in the TAD system, or whether a Certificado Veterinario Internacional can be processed for a non-commercial captive-bred specimen with a biosecurity plan.
kit.branch_note: Lever = the AGENCY (Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad), NOT the legislature. No statute names or bans R. rattus by species; the prohibition flows entirely from an administrative classification (EEI-1 under Resolución 109/2021, a Ministerio de Ambiente resolution) and its Art. 5 operative ban. Because the barrier is the agency's own classification and the absence of a formal domestication/captive-bred exception, the fix is administrative: Art. 6 of Res. 109/2021 contemplates regulated exceptions, and the directorate already exercises de-facto interpretive discretion by treating R. norvegicus as domestic. So there is no hostile statute to repeal and nothing to take to Congress — pushing the legislature would solve a problem that doesn't exist on paper. Federal-vs-provincial dimension: the federal government controls inter-provincial commerce, imports, and the EEI list, but the police power over the contents of a private home falls to provinces/municipalities, so even a favorable national clarification on tenencia would not bind a province that chooses to enact a stricter local ban — this is a federal-first ask whose protection is reinforced, not replaced, by keeping breeder/captive-origin paperwork.

targets.name: Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (Subsecretaría de Ambiente, Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible)
targets.why: The national environmental Application Authority that maintains the EEI list (Res. 109/2021), enforces the Art. 5 prohibitions, runs the fauna-operator registry (RPUOFS, Res. 170/2021), and holds the pre-import authorization power over wildlife. It is the only office that can issue a written clarification on tenencia and grant or interpret an Art. 6 exception extending captive-bred R. rattus the de-facto domestic treatment already given to R. norvegicus. rpuofs@ambiente.gob.ar is the directorate's wildlife-operator inbox; mesadeentradas@ambiente.gob.ar is the general entry desk.

targets.name: SENASA — Dirección de Comercio Exterior Animal (Mascotas No Tradicionales)
targets.why: The national animal-health service that runs the import protocol for non-traditional pets (CVI, SIGTrámites/TAD). Sanitary clearance is subordinate to the environmental veto, so SENASA is the right office to ask whether an EEI-1 companion rodent is auto-rejected in TAD or whether a CVI can be processed for a non-commercial captive-bred specimen. responde@senasa.gob.ar is the confirmed general inbox; dcea@senasa.gob.ar reaches the foreign-animal-trade directorate.

template.en:
To the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (Subsecretaría de Ambiente):

I am writing as a private hobbyist regarding the regulatory status of the roof rat (Rattus rattus) kept as an indoor companion animal. I understand the species is listed as a Category 1 Invasive Exotic Species (EEI-1) under Resolución 109/2021, and that Article 5 prohibits its breeding, sale, donation, release, import, and inter-jurisdictional movement.

I have two questions and one request for clarification.

First, on possession (tenencia): Article 5 enumerates the banned activities but does not include passive private possession. Could you confirm in writing that simply keeping a pre-existing, captive-bred R. rattus indoors — never released into the environment — is not among the activities prohibited by Article 5?

Second, on parity with the fancy rat: Rattus norvegicus carries the identical EEI-1 listing, yet its captive-bred laboratory and fancy strains are bred, transported, and sold openly nationwide because they are treated in practice as domestic animals (animales domésticos) outside the wildlife regime. R. rattus born and raised in captivity to captive parents is, in every practical husbandry sense, indistinguishable and equally non-releasable. Does any formal regulatory exception exist — via Article 6 of Resolución 109/2021, an internal dictamen, or administrative jurisprudence — that could extend to documented, closed-colony, captive-bred R. rattus the same domestic-animal treatment already afforded de facto to R. norvegicus, so that such specimens fall outside the EEI-1 commercialization and transport prohibitions?

I am asking purely to understand the regulatory framework and to keep any animal lawfully and responsibly. Thank you for your time and guidance.

[Your name]
[Your contact details]
template.es:
A la Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (Subsecretaría de Ambiente):

Me dirijo a ustedes como aficionado/a particular respecto de la situación regulatoria de la rata de techo (Rattus rattus) tenida como animal de compañía dentro del hogar. Entiendo que la especie está clasificada como Especie Exótica Invasora Categoría 1 (EEI-1) en el Anexo I de la Resolución 109/2021, y que su Artículo 5 prohíbe su cría, compra y venta, donación, liberación, introducción al territorio nacional y movimiento interjurisdiccional.

Formulo dos consultas y una solicitud de aclaración.

Primero, sobre la tenencia: el Artículo 5 enumera las actividades prohibidas pero no incluye la tenencia o posesión particular pasiva. ¿Podrían confirmarme por escrito que la mera tenencia de un ejemplar de R. rattus ya existente, nacido en cautiverio y mantenido íntegramente en el interior de la vivienda —sin liberación al ambiente— no se encuentra entre las actividades prohibidas por el Artículo 5?

Segundo, sobre la paridad con la rata doméstica común: Rattus norvegicus figura con idéntica clasificación EEI-1, y sin embargo sus cepas de laboratorio y domésticas criadas en cautiverio se crían, transportan y venden abiertamente en todo el país porque, en la práctica, se las trata como animales domésticos fuera del régimen de fauna silvestre. Un ejemplar de R. rattus nacido y criado en cautiverio, hijo de padres también criados en cautiverio, es en todo sentido práctico de manejo indistinguible e igualmente no liberable. ¿Existe alguna excepción reglamentaria formal —vía Artículo 6 de la Resolución 109/2021, un dictamen interno o jurisprudencia administrativa— que pueda extender a los ejemplares documentados de R. rattus, de colonia cerrada y criados en cautiverio, el mismo tratamiento de 'animal doméstico' que de hecho ya se otorga a R. norvegicus, de modo que tales ejemplares queden fuera de las prohibiciones de comercialización y transporte propias de la categoría EEI-1?

Mi consulta tiene como único fin comprender el marco regulatorio y poder tener cualquier animal de manera lícita y responsable. Desde ya, agradezco su tiempo y orientación.

[Su nombre]
[Sus datos de contacto]

kit.confidence_notes: Grounded in the Gemini DR (2026-06-10). The operative ban is Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 (verbatim: 'Prohíbase la introducción al territorio nacional y el movimiento interjurisdiccional de las especies clasificadas como de uso restringido, así como su cría o cultivo, compra y venta, donación y liberación en lugares sometidos a jurisdicción nacional'), which omits 'tenencia' — the basis for the possession gray zone under Const. Nacional Art. 19. The R. norvegicus de-facto domestication exemption is documented but uncodified (no formal carve-out names it), which is precisely why the keep status is unregulated_unclear and why a written clarification/Art. 6 exception is the ask. Art. 6 of Res. 109/2021 as an exception vehicle is inferred from the resolution's structure (DR §E frames the inquiry around 'Art. 6, dictamen interno, o jurisprudencia administrativa') and should be confirmed by the agency. Email/phone channels (rpuofs@ambiente.gob.ar, mesadeentradas@ambiente.gob.ar, responde@senasa.gob.ar, dcea@senasa.gob.ar, +54 11 4318-7400/7500, +54 9 11 3585 9810) and TAD form URLs are taken from the DR's Section F agency contacts. Province-level rules vary and were not individually verified; a favorable federal clarification would not bind a province that enacts a stricter local ban.

keep.why: Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 enumerates the banned activities for EEI-1 species — cría, compra/venta, donación, liberación, introducción al territorio nacional, and movimiento interjurisdiccional — but conspicuously omits 'tenencia' (passive private possession). Under the constitutional legality principle (Const. Nacional Art. 19: no inhabitant may be deprived of what the law does not forbid), merely keeping a pre-existing captive-bred R. rattus indoors is not an enumerated federal offense, so federal authorities have no Art. 5 mandate to confiscate it. This is a jurisprudential gap, not an affirmative protected right: provinces and municipalities retain the police power to enact stricter local bans on keeping invasive rodents, and federal silence does not equal permission. Treat as unregulated/unclear — neither expressly authorized nor expressly prohibited.
keep.governing_law: Resolución 109/2021 Art. 5 (EEI-1 ban list — 'tenencia' omitted); Constitución Nacional Art. 19 (principio de legalidad); Ley 22.421 Art. 3 (fauna silvestre definition reaches captive-bred exotics).

breed.why: Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 expressly prohibits 'su cría o cultivo' for EEI-1 species in places under national jurisdiction, with no hobbyist or small-breeder threshold. Because R. rattus is EEI-1, the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad is legally stripped of authority to grant any breeding license, and the Art. 5 ban preempts the fauna-operator registry (RPUOFS, Res. 170/2021) — so even a fully compliant criadero application would be administratively dead on arrival. There is no lawful private or commercial pathway to breed the species; any breeding is treated as an illicit act of wildlife trafficking. (By contrast, R. norvegicus is bred openly under a de-facto domestication exemption that R. rattus does not share.)
breed.governing_law: Resolución 109/2021 Art. 5 ('Prohíbase... su cría o cultivo... de las especies clasificadas como de uso restringido'); Res. 170/2021 (RPUOFS — preempted/foreclosed for EEI-1); Ley 22.421 Art. 3.

sell_give.why: Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 expressly prohibits 'compra y venta, donación' of EEI-1 species — covering both sale and non-commercial gifting/donation. There is no lawful avenue to commercialize or transfer R. rattus: the Art. 5 ban preempts the fauna-operator registry (Res. 170/2021), so no dealer/criadero license can issue, and even gifting is enumerated as a banned act. This forecloses any private give-away as well as commercial sale. (R. norvegicus is sold openly only because of an uncodified de-facto domestication exemption that R. rattus does not formally enjoy.)
sell_give.governing_law: Resolución 109/2021 Art. 5 ('Prohíbase... compra y venta, donación... de las especies clasificadas como de uso restringido'); Res. 170/2021 (RPUOFS — foreclosed for EEI-1); Ley 22.421 Art. 9.

transport.why: Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 imposes a blanket ban on 'la introducción al territorio nacional y el movimiento interjurisdiccional' of EEI-1 species, so both importing R. rattus and moving it across provincial lines are prohibited. On import, the SENASA sanitary pathway (CVI, TAD, SIGTrámites) is entirely subordinate to the environmental veto: the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad must authorize a wildlife import first (Decreto 666/1997 Art. 22 empowers it to reject ecologically harmful imports), and for an EEI-1 species it is obligated to refuse — so SENASA can never issue the final entry permit. Internally, provincial fauna authorities cannot issue a transit guide (guía de tránsito) for a federally restricted EEI-1 species for personal relocation, leaving the animal legally trapped in its current province. No lawful transport pathway exists. (Intra-provincial movement within a single jurisdiction is not reached by the inter-jurisdictional ban, but the keep status governs there.)
transport.governing_law: Resolución 109/2021 Art. 5 (ban on introducción al territorio nacional + movimiento interjurisdiccional); Decreto 666/1997 Art. 22 (rejection of harmful live-animal imports); SENASA import protocol (mascotas no tradicionales — subordinate to environmental authorization); Ley 22.421.

restrictions.summary: Because R. rattus is a Category 1 Invasive Exotic Species (EEI-1), Art. 5 of Resolución 109/2021 bans breeding (cría), purchase/sale, donation, release (liberación), importation, and inter-jurisdictional movement, with no lawful permit pathway — the EEI-1 status strips the wildlife directorate of authority to license the species and preempts the fauna-operator registry (Res. 170/2021). Passive private possession ('tenencia') is not on the Art. 5 ban list, but a possessor is then locked in: cannot lawfully breed it, give it away, sell its offspring, or move it across provinces. Provinces/municipalities may add stricter local bans. Never release — liberation is expressly prohibited.
steps: Do NOT breed, sell, give away, import, or move R. rattus across provincial lines — these are banned for EEI-1 species (Res. 109/2021 Art. 5)
Never release a roof rat into the environment (liberación is expressly prohibited)

If advocating: ask the Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad for a written clarification on tenencia and a possible Art. 6 exception extending R. norvegicus-style domestic treatment to captive-bred R. rattus
restrictions.where_to_file: Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad (Subsecretaría de Ambiente) for clarifications/exceptions; SENASA for import questions; provincial fauna authority for transit

inquiry_focus: (1) El Artículo 5 de la Resolución 109/2021 prohíbe la cría, compra/venta, donación, liberación, introducción y movimiento interjurisdiccional de las EEI-1, pero omite la 'tenencia'. ¿Confirma la Dirección Nacional de Biodiversidad que la mera tenencia particular de un ejemplar de Rattus rattus ya existente, nacido en cautiverio y no liberado, queda fuera de las prohibiciones del Art. 5 (conforme al principio de legalidad, Const. Nacional Art. 19)? (2) Dado que R. rattus y R. norvegicus figuran idénticamente como EEI-1 y que R. norvegicus se cría y comercializa abiertamente bajo un trato de facto como animal doméstico, ¿existe alguna excepción reglamentaria formal —vía Art. 6 de la Res. 109/2021, dictamen interno o jurisprudencia administrativa— que extienda ese trato de 'animal doméstico' a los ejemplares documentados de R. rattus criados en cautiverio, de colonia cerrada? (3) Para la importación de un R. rattus criado en cautiverio como mascota, ¿SENASA rechaza automáticamente la solicitud en TAD por la clasificación EEI-1 (Res. 109/2021 + Decreto 666/1997 Art. 22), o es administrativamente posible tramitar el CVI sin fines comerciales y con un plan de bioseguridad?
